name: Uto-Aztecan
summary: About thirty languages stretching from Idaho and Oregon to El Salvador. They include Nahuatl, the language of the Aztec empire; Hopi of the Arizona mesas; Comanche, Shoshone and Paiute of the Great Basin and Plains; and Yaqui, Rarámuri and O'odham of the Sonoran borderlands. It is one of the best-established language families of the Americas, although where it began, among desert foragers or among early maize farmers, is still argued.

sources.citation: Hammarström, Harald, Robert Forkel, Martin Haspelmath & Sebastian Bank. Glottolog: Uto-Aztecan (utoa1244).
Campbell, Lyle. 1997. American Indian Languages: The Historical Linguistics of Native America. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

essay.title: From Buschmann to Sapir
essay.body:
The first person to see the outlines of the family was the German philologist Johann Carl Eduard Buschmann, who in 1859 published a vast survey of the languages of northern Mexico and the American West. He recognised that the languages of Sonora and those the Americans would later call Shoshonean belonged together, and he noticed a great many resemblances to Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs. But he explained the Nahuatl likenesses as borrowings from a prestigious neighbour, not as signs of common descent.

The name came in 1891, when the American anthropologist Daniel Brinton grouped Ute, the Sonoran languages and Aztec into a single 'Uto-Aztecan' stock. Brinton's case rested on lists of similar words, and for two decades it was not clear that the similarities were more than chance and contact. Alfred Kroeber, working on the languages of California, sorted the northern languages into subgroups in 1907, but the question of Nahuatl's place remained open.

It was settled by Edward Sapir. Between 1913 and 1919 he published a comparison of Southern Paiute and Nahuatl that did for Uto-Aztecan what Grimm and his successors had done for Indo-European. He set out regular sound correspondences: Nahuatl had lost Proto-Uto-Aztecan `*p` at the start of a word, and turned `*t` into *tl* before *a*, while Southern Paiute kept both. Once the differences could be predicted, borrowing was no longer a credible explanation. Sapir's study was also one of the first demonstrations that the comparative method works on languages with no old written records.

Later work filled in the detail. Benjamin Whorf refined the sound laws in the 1930s, Wick Miller published a standard list of cognate sets in 1967, Ronald Langacker reconstructed much of the grammar in the 1970s, and Brian Stubbs's comparative vocabulary of 2011 gathered more than two thousand cognate sets.

essay.title: Deserts, Maize and a Homeland in Dispute
essay.body:
Proto-Uto-Aztecan is usually dated to around five thousand years ago, though estimates based on the amount of divergence are rough. Where it was spoken is one of the most argued homeland questions in the Americas, because the answer decides whether the family spread with farming or without it.

The older view looks north. Catherine Fowler's study of reconstructed plant and animal names in 1983 found words for plants and animals of upland and desert country, such as pines and several desert plants, and she placed the homeland in the region between southern California, the Great Basin and the Southwest. On this view the ancestors were foragers, and the southern branches moved down the western side of Mexico later, taking up maize farming as they went or on arrival.

In 2001 Jane Hill turned the picture round. She argued that a set of words for maize, grinding and cultivation could be reconstructed for the whole family, and that Proto-Uto-Aztecan speakers were therefore early cultivators in western or central Mexico. Their languages would then have spread north with maize, which reached the American Southwest by about 2000 BCE, in the way that farming is thought to have carried Bantu or Austronesian languages.

The linguistic evidence has been contested on its own terms. In 2009 William Merrill and colleagues reviewed the maize vocabulary and argued that it can be securely reconstructed only for **Southern Uto-Aztecan**, not for the family as a whole, which fits a northern homeland better. Archaeology dates the arrival of maize in the Southwest well enough, but cannot by itself say what language its first farmers spoke, and genetic studies of living populations have not produced a clear answer either. Most specialists now treat both scenarios as open.

essay.title: A Family Likeness
essay.body:
Proto-Uto-Aztecan had a modest sound system: five vowels, including a high central vowel written `*ï`, and consonants with no contrast between voiced and voiceless stops. Much of the diversity of the modern languages comes from what happened to a few of these sounds. `*p` stayed in **Hopi** and **Numic**, softened to *b* in Yaqui and *v* in O'odham, and vanished at the start of words in Nahuatl. `*y` became *d* in O'odham. Numic languages add their own twist with consonant gradation and whispered, voiceless vowels at the ends of words.

The grammar is built mostly with suffixes and postpositions. Langacker reconstructed a verb-final word order for the proto-language, and Hopi, the Numic languages and Yaqui still put the verb last. O'odham and Nahuatl have moved away from this: O'odham word order is notably free, and Nahuatl tends to put the verb early. Many nouns carried a suffix, reconstructed as `*-ta`, that marked the plain, unpossessed form. In Nahuatl it survives as the familiar *-tl*, *-tli* or *-li*: *calli* 'house' but *nocal* 'my house'.

Two other habits recur across the family. Plurals are often made by repeating the first syllable, as in Classical Nahuatl *coyōtl* 'coyote', plural *cōcoyoh*. And several languages build nouns into the verb: Nahuatl *nitlacua* 'I eat (something)', with a general object prefix, beside *ninacacua* 'I eat meat', with *naca-* 'meat' incorporated.

None of the languages had a full writing system before Europeans arrived. The Aztecs used a system of pictures and signs that could spell out names by the rebus principle, but not whole sentences. Nahuatl was written in the Latin alphabet within a few years of the conquest, and practical alphabets for Hopi, O'odham, Yaqui and the Numic languages came only in the 20th century.

essay.title: Unsettled Questions
essay.body:
That the family exists is not in doubt. How its branches fit together is less certain. Most classifications recognise eight or so well-defined groups: **Numic**, **Takic**, **Hopi** and Tübatulabal in the north, and **Tepiman**, **Taracahitan**, Corachol and **Aztecan** in the south. Above that level, agreement fades. A **Southern Uto-Aztecan** branch is supported by shared words and sound changes and is widely accepted. A **Northern Uto-Aztecan** branch is more doubtful. Wick Miller's word counts grouped the northern languages together, but Lyle Campbell, Ronald Langacker and others have pointed out that shared features among neighbours can come from centuries of contact as well as from a common ancestor.

Within the south, Taracahitan may not be a single branch at all, and some scholars join Corachol (Cora and Huichol) with Aztecan in a Corachol-Aztecan group. The internal diversity of Nahuatl, which is a dialect continuum large enough to be counted as several languages, raises its own questions of classification.

The dating debate is tied to the homeland debate. A proto-language of the Mexican cultivators in Hill's model cannot be much older than the domestication of maize, while a northern forager homeland imposes no such limit. Neither camp can yet point to a decisive date.

The search for relatives beyond the family has been less successful. In 1937 Benjamin Whorf and George Trager proposed that Uto-Aztecan was related to the Kiowa-Tanoan languages of the Plains and the Rio Grande pueblos, forming an Aztec-Tanoan stock, and Sapir included it in his larger proposals of the 1920s. A few suggestive resemblances have been noted, but no regular sound correspondences have been demonstrated, and most specialists regard Aztec-Tanoan as unproven. Uto-Aztecan is therefore treated as an independent family.
